# Universal machine and the limits of computation (`turing_machine_computability`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: needs algorithm_concept; helped by formal_logic, boolean_logic
- Core idea: Everything that can be calculated by rule can be calculated by an extremely simple device: a tape of squares, a head that reads and writes one symbol at a time and moves one square left or right, and a finite table that says what to do for each combination of internal state and symbol read. Such a table can itself be written on the tape as symbols, and one fixed machine, the universal machine, can read any table and imitate it; this is the idea of software. There are also exactly stated problems that no machine can ever solve: no procedure can decide for every program and input whether it will eventually stop. The proof assumes such a tester exists and feeds it a program built to do the opposite of what the tester predicts about it.
- Pitfalls:
  - Taking the tape machine for a design to be built; it is a yardstick for what can be computed at all
  - Concluding that computers can therefore solve everything given enough time and memory
  - Concluding the opposite, that undecidability makes program testing pointless; it only rules out a method that works for all programs
  - Confusing what cannot be computed at all with what merely takes too long
- History: europe: 1928 – Hilbert and Ackermann formulate the decision problem for first-order logic; 1931 Gödel's incompleteness theorems (Vienna); 1936 Turing, On Computable Numbers (Cambridge); americas: 1936 – Church's lambda calculus and unsolvable problem, and Post's similar machine, both independent of Turing (Princeton, New York)
- Read:
  - Alan M. Turing, On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society 42 (1936–1937)
  - Charles Petzold, The Annotated Turing (2008)
